explanation: Simple Past regular: verb + -ed. "play -> played", "walk -> walked", "jump -> jumped". If verb ends in -e: just add -d (love -> loved).
options: Add -ing to the verb (play -> playing, walk -> walking)
Add -s to the verb (play -> plays, walk -> walks)
Add -ed to the verb (play -> played, walk -> walked)
Add -es to the verb (go -> goes, watch -> watches)
question: How do you form the Simple Past of regular verbs?

explanation: "Go" is irregular: go -> went -> gone. "I went to school yesterday." (Simple Past) vs. "I have gone" (Present Perfect).
options: goed
went
gone
goes
question: Which is the correct Simple Past of "go"?

explanation: "Write" is irregular: write -> wrote -> written. "She wrote a letter yesterday." (Simple Past) vs. "She has written..." (Present Perfect).
options: writed
wrote
written
wrotes
question: Which is the correct Simple Past of "write"?

explanation: "Take" is irregular: take -> took -> taken. "He took the book yesterday." (Simple Past).
options: taked
tooken
took
taken
question: Which is the correct Simple Past of "take"?

explanation: Present Progressive: am/is/are + Verb + -ing. "I am reading." "She is watching TV." "They are playing." Used for: actions happening now, temporary situations.
options: Subject + will + infinitive (I will read)
Subject + have + past participle (I have read)
Subject + am/is/are + verb + -ing (I am reading)
Subject + verb + -s (She reads a book)
question: How do you form the Present Progressive (Verlaufsform)?

explanation: Present Progressive: 1) now: "I am eating." 2) temporary: "She is living in London for a year." 3) near future plans: "We are meeting tomorrow."
options: For permanent facts and general truths (Water freezes at 0 degrees)
For actions happening around now (I am studying this week)
For finished past events at a named time (We visited Rome in 2019)
For plans that are still uncertain (Maybe I will travel)
question: When do we use the Present Progressive?

explanation: Simple Present: habits (I usually get up at 7). Facts (The earth orbits the sun). Progressive: now (She is calling you) or temporary (He is working in Paris this month).
options: There is no real difference; both tenses can always be exchanged
Simple Present: habits and facts. Progressive: happening now
Simple Present is the politer form and is used in formal speech
The Progressive is used in writing only, the Simple Present in speech
question: What is the difference between Simple Present and Present Progressive?

explanation: Simple Past question: Did + subject + infinitive (no -ed!). "Did you go to school?" "Did she write the letter?" Do NOT say: "Did you went?"
options: Verb + subject + ? (Went you to school yesterday?)
Did + subject + infinitive? (Did you see the film yesterday?)
Have + subject + past participle? (Have you gone there?)
Will + subject + infinitive? (Will you go there?)
question: How do you form a question in Simple Past?

explanation: Simple Past negative: didn't + infinitive (NOT past tense). "I didn't see him." (NOT: "I didn't saw him") "She didn't go." (NOT: "She didn't went")
options: Subject + no + past tense verb (I no saw him)
Subject + didn't + infinitive (I didn't see him)
Subject + not + past tense verb (I not saw him yesterday)
Subject + wasn't + infinitive (I wasn't go)
question: How do you form a negative in Simple Past?

explanation: Present Perfect (have/has + Partizip II): 1) Erfahrungen: "I have been to Paris." 2) Ergebnis der Vergangenheit relevant jetzt: "She has lost her key." 3) Mit yet, already, just, ever, never.
options: Only for finished actions at a named past time (last Tuesday, in 1990)
For experiences and results that matter now (She has just arrived)
Only for future events that are already planned (next week, tomorrow)
For habits that happen again and again (every day, on Mondays)
question: What is the Present Perfect used for?

explanation: Present Perfect: have/has + Partizip II (3. Form). "I have eaten." "She has gone." "They have played." Regular past participle: verb + -ed. Irregular: go/went/gone, see/saw/seen.
options: Subject + will + infinitive (She will go to school)
Subject + have/has + 3rd form (I have eaten)
Subject + am/is/are + -ing (She is going home now)
Subject + did + infinitive (She did go yesterday)
question: How do you form the Present Perfect?

explanation: "Used to" + infinitive: früherer Zustand/Gewohnheit, die jetzt nicht mehr gilt. "I used to eat meat but now I am vegetarian." Nur in der Vergangenheit!
options: A future habit that will be repeated regularly (I will go every day)
A past habit or state that no longer exists (I used to play piano, but not any more)
A present habit that happens regularly and has not changed (I play piano)
A polite request directed at someone else (Could you help me?)
question: What does "used to" express?

explanation: Comparatives: zwei Dinge vergleichen. Short adjectives: -er. "tall -> taller". Long adjectives: more. "beautiful -> more beautiful". "than" = als.
options: To say that something is the highest in a group (the superlative)
To compare two things (She is taller than her brother)
To describe a noun more exactly (a very big house)
To ask about qualities (How tall is he?)
question: What are comparative adjectives used for?

explanation: "Good" is irregular: good -> better -> best. "This book is better than that one." Common irregular: good/better/best, bad/worse/worst, many/more/most, little/less/least.
options: gooder
more good
better
goodest
question: How do you form the comparative of "good"?

explanation: Long adjectives (3+ syllables): most + adjective. "most interesting". Short adjectives: -est. "big -> biggest". "beautiful -> most beautiful".
options: interestinger
most interesting
interestingest
more interesting
question: How do you form the superlative of "interesting"?

explanation: "Going to" future: am/is/are + going to + infinitive. "I am going to visit Paris next year." Used for plans and intentions, or when evidence shows something will happen.
options: Subject + going to + past tense verb (I going to walked home yesterday)
Subject + am/is/are + going to + infinitive (I am going to travel)
Subject + will + going + infinitive (I will going visit Paris next year)
Subject + to + going + infinitive (I to going visit Rome)
question: How do you express the future with "going to"?

explanation: "I will help you!" (spontane Entscheidung). "I am going to visit Rome next summer." (Plan steht schon fest). Both are future but with different nuances.
options: There is no difference at all; both forms can always be exchanged freely
Will: spontaneous decisions or predictions. Going to: fixed plans
Will is only used in written English, going to only in spoken English
Going to describes past plans, while will describes present intentions
question: What is the difference between "will" and "going to"?

explanation: Conditional I (reale Bedingung): If + Simple Present, will + infinitive. "If the weather is nice, we will go swimming." Reale/mögliche Bedingung.
options: If + Simple Past, would + infinitive (If it rained, I would stay)
If + Simple Present, will + infinitive (If it rains, we will stay at home)
If + Past Perfect, would have + past participle (If it had rained, I would have stayed)
If + will + infinitive, will + infinitive (If it will rain, I will stay)
question: How do you form conditional sentences type 1 (real condition)?

explanation: Conditional II (irreale Bedingung): If + Simple Past, would + infinitive. "If I were rich, I would help everyone." Irreale/unwahrscheinliche Bedingung.
options: If + Simple Present, will + infinitive (If I have money, I will travel)
If + Simple Past, would + infinitive (If I had a million euros, I would travel the world)
If + Present Perfect, would have + past participle (If I have saved, I would travel)
If + Future, will + infinitive (If I will have money, I will travel)
question: How do you form conditional sentences type 2 (unreal condition)?

explanation: Relative clause: "The girl who lives next door is my friend." who = für Personen, which = für Dinge, that = für beides. where = Ort, when = Zeit.
options: A clause that says when something happens, using when or while (when I was young)
A clause that adds information about a noun (The book that I read was good)
A clause that describes an unreal situation with if (If I were rich, I would travel)
A clause that gives a purpose (so that she could win)
question: What is a relative clause?

explanation: "Who" = für Personen. "The man who called is my uncle." "The girl who wrote the letter." Compare: which/that = für Sachen.
options: For things and objects (The book who I read was interesting)
For people (The teacher who taught us)
For places (The city who I visited last summer)
For times (The day who we met was sunny)
question: When do we use "who" in a relative clause?

explanation: Passive voice: "The letter was written by her." Passive: am/is/are/was/were + past participle. Aktiv betont den Handlungsträger, Passiv betont das Ergebnis.
options: She wrote a long letter to her aunt.
The letter was written by her.
She is writing a letter to her friend.
She had written the letter last week.
question: Which sentence uses the passive voice?

explanation: Simple Present Passive: am/is/are + past participle. "English is spoken here." "Milk is sold in shops." "Books are printed in factories."
options: Subject + have been + past participle (have been built)
Subject + is/are + being + past participle (is being built)
Subject + am/is/are + past participle (is built, are sold)
Subject + will + past participle (It will built)
question: How do you form the passive in Simple Present?

explanation: Modal verbs: can (können), could (könnte), must (muss), should (sollte), may (darf), might (könnte), will (wird), would (würde). Modals have no -s in 3rd person and are followed by infinitive.
options: Regular verbs that follow the normal rules (play -> plays -> played)
Auxiliary verbs for ability, permission or obligation (can, must, should, may, might)
Irregular verbs whose past forms must be learnt by heart (go -> went -> gone)
Verbs that always end in -ing and describe ongoing actions (running, eating)
question: What are modal verbs?

explanation: "Must" = interne Notwendigkeit/Regel. "I must study" (ich fühle die Pflicht). "Have to" = externe Notwendigkeit. "I have to wear a uniform" (Schule schreibt es vor). Often interchangeable.
options: Must and have to always mean different things and can never be exchanged
Must: personal obligation. Have to: obligation from outside.
Must is the past tense form of have to and describes past obligations
Have to is always more polite and more formal than must
question: How do you express obligation with "must" vs "have to"?

explanation: "Should" = sollte, Empfehlung. "You should see a doctor." "He shouldn't eat so much sugar." Weaker than must. Used for advice.
options: Certainty - something will definitely happen (It will rain tomorrow)
Advice or a recommendation (You should eat more fruit)
Obligation - a strict rule you must follow (You must wear a helmet)
Permission - giving someone the right to do something (You may go now)
question: What does "should" express?

explanation: Questions: 1) with auxiliaries (be, have, can): invert subject and auxiliary. "Is she happy?" 2) Simple Present/Past: do/does/did + subject + infinitive. "Do you know her?"
options: Just add a question mark to a statement (You like pizza?)
Use do/does/did or an auxiliary before the subject (Do you like pizza?)
Put the main verb at the very end, as in German (You pizza like?)
Always start with the subject and then the verb, as in a statement (You like pizza?)
question: How do you form questions in English?

explanation: Tag questions: am Satzende angefügt. Positive statement -> negative tag. "It's cold, isn't it?" Negative statement -> positive tag. "You don't know, do you?"
options: Very long questions that ask for a lot of information (Where did you go?)
Short questions added to a statement to confirm it (It's nice, isn't it? / You can swim, can't you?)
Questions that begin with why and ask for a reason (Why are you late?)
Questions that begin with how and ask about the manner (How did you do that?)
question: What are tag questions?

explanation: "Neither...nor" = weder...noch. Negative alternative. "I have neither a pen nor a pencil." Compare: "either...or" = entweder...oder.
options: An alternative choice - one of two options is possible (either ... or)
Two negatives - not the one and not the other (Neither he nor she)
Both possibilities - two things are true at the same time (both ... and)
A limitation - only one single thing is allowed (only ...)
question: What does "neither...nor" express?

explanation: Reported speech: "He said he was tired." (Direct: "I am tired.") Tense shifts back: am -> was, will -> would, can -> could. "that" verbindet.
options: Direct speech - repeating the exact words in quotation marks (I am tired)
Indirect speech - telling what someone said (He said he was tired)
A question that asks someone to repeat what they just said (Sorry?)
A command that tells someone to do something at once (Close the door!)
question: What is reported speech?

explanation: "I agree with you." Correct. NOT "I am agree" (agree is NOT used with progressive form). State verbs: agree, know, understand, believe, like, love -> no progressive.
options: I am agree with you
I agree with you
I am agreeing with you
I am agreed with you
question: Which sentence is correct?

explanation: State verbs: beschreiben Zustände, nicht Handlungen. NICHT im Progressive: "I know" (NOT "I am knowing"). "I like" (NOT "I am liking"). "She owns a car" (NOT "she is owning").
options: Action verbs that describe movement or activity (run, jump, swim, dance)
Verbs that describe a state, not an action, and take no -ing form (know, like, own)
Irregular verbs whose past tense and past participle must be learnt by heart (go, went, gone)
Modal verbs that express ability or obligation (can, must, should, may)
question: What are "stative verbs" (Zustandsverben)?

explanation: "As well as" = sowohl...als auch / sowie. "She can sing as well as dance." "He likes history as well as geography." Adds information.
options: aber / however - introducing a contrast to what was just said (but, however)
sowie / ebenfalls - adding extra information (She plays piano as well as guitar)
weder ... noch - saying that neither of two things is true (neither, nor)
entweder ... oder - presenting two alternatives to choose from (either, or)
question: What does "as well as" mean?

explanation: "Although/Even though" = obwohl. "Although she was tired, she continued working." "Even though it was expensive, he bought it." Introduces a concessive clause.
options: To give a reason for something that happened (because, since, as)
To express a contrast (Although it was raining, we went outside)
To describe the result of a previous action (so, therefore, that is why)
To express a time relationship (when, while, before, after)
question: How do you use "although/even though"?

explanation: "Unless" = es sei denn / wenn nicht. "I'll help you unless you are rude." = "I'll help you if you are NOT rude." Unless + positive condition = negative meaning.
options: wenn / if - introducing a simple condition (If it rains, I will stay at home)
es sei denn dass / wenn nicht (I will come unless it rains tomorrow)
weil / because - giving a reason (because it was late)
obwohl / although - introducing a contrast (although it was late)
question: What does "unless" mean?

explanation: Frequency adverbs (always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never): before main verb ("I often read") but after "be" ("She is always tired").
options: Always at the very end of the sentence, after the object (I read books often)
Usually before the main verb, but after be (She is always late)
Always at the very beginning, before the subject (Often I read books)
Only in questions, never in normal statements (Do you often read?)
question: How are adverbs of frequency used?

explanation: "Much" + uncountable: "much water, much time, much money." "Many" + countable (plural): "many books, many people, many hours." In affirmative sentences often: a lot of.
options: There is no difference; both words work with every kind of noun (much books)
Much: for uncountable nouns. Many: for countable nouns (much water, many books)
Much is the polite form, many is used in everyday speech (many time)
Many is used only in questions, much only in statements (How many water?)
question: What is the difference between "much" and "many"?

explanation: "A few" = ein paar (zählbar): "a few books, a few friends." "A little" = ein wenig (unzählbar): "a little water, a little time." Both are slightly positive (some, not much).
options: There is no difference; both words mean exactly the same thing in every context
A few: a small number (countable). A little: a small amount (uncountable)
A few is negative and means that almost nothing at all is left (a few money)
A little means none at all - there is zero amount of something left
question: What is the difference between "a few" and "a little"?

explanation: Gerund: Verb + -ing als Nomen. "Swimming is my hobby." (Subjekt). "She enjoys reading." (Objekt nach enjoys, like, love, hate, avoid, finish, suggest). After prepositions.
options: Verb + -ed, so that the past tense form is used as a noun (played is my hobby)
Verb + -ing, used as a subject or an object (Swimming is fun)
Verb + -s, the third person form used as a noun (plays)
Verb + -tion, making a noun from a verb (information)
question: How do you form the gerund (-ing form used as noun)?

explanation: Verben die Gerund verlangen: enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest, mind, keep, imagine, miss, practise, consider. "I enjoy swimming." "She avoids eating sugar." "Mind = stört es dich?"
options: After to, want and would like (I want to swim / I would like to go home)
After enjoy, avoid, finish, mind (I enjoy swimming / She avoids sugar)
After will, would, can and must (modals are followed by the bare infinitive)
After hope, decide, promise (I hope to win / She decided to leave)
question: After which verbs do we usually use a gerund (-ing)?

explanation: "Whereas" = wohingegen, während hingegen. Drückt einen Kontrast aus. "Some people are morning persons, whereas others prefer evenings." Ähnlich: while, in contrast to.
options: weil / because - giving the reason for something that happened (because it rained)
wohingegen / während - expressing a contrast (She likes tea, he likes coffee)
obwohl / although - showing something unexpected (although it was cold)
damit / so that - expressing a purpose (so that she could win)
question: What does "whereas" mean?
